source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis (Memory & Cognition 45)
finding: The headline numbers are now verified from the full text. Experts keep a moderate recall edge on shuffled material in chess, music, programming, sports and other domains. The edge is probably overstated by publication bias.
numbers: 45 studies (1,401 participants, 55 samples) in a sign test; 24 studies with usable data = 28 samples, 28 effect sizes, N=903. Random-effects mean r=.41, 95% CI [.29,.51], I2=63.06%. Trim-and-fill (8 studies filled): r=.29 [.17,.41]. Fail-safe N=745. Without 2 questionable samples (k=26): r=.39 [.28,.50]. By domain: games r=.42 (k=11), music .69 (k=5), programming .36 (k=6), sports .30 (k=3, CI crosses 0), other .24 (k=3, CI crosses 0); domain moderator Q(4)=8.69, p=.069. Exposure time (<=8 s vs >8 s) not a moderator, p=.346.
quote: the presence of publication bias suggests that the overall correlation ... is probably an overestimation
limits: Small k; no moderators for age or expertise level; a Gobet-group paper (theory-friendly). Correlation across skill levels, not a per-item effect size.
agent_relevance: Plan on a real but modest residual gain from stored patterns on shuffled input (r about .3 to .4). Use .29 as the planning value.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory (Cognitive Science 24), Table 1 re-read from the paper text
finding: The growth-curve constants quoted in claim K07 were checked against Table 1 of the paper text and match. Skill raises both the 1-s start and the later rate.
numbers: P=100-B*exp(-c(t-1)). Game positions: Class A B=75.176 (ASE 3.227), c=.033; Experts B=66.414, c=.074; Masters B=29.240 (CI 19.3-39.2), c=.435 (CI .089-.781). Random: Class A B=90.617, c=.006; Experts B=85.338, c=.012; Masters B=80.539, c=.018. Text: c rises x2 (A to Exp) and x15 (A to Masters); amount learned in 1 s (100-B) rises x1.3 and nearly x3. Masters at 10 s average 92.4%; 3 of 5 Masters above 96%, 2 at about 85%. Masters r2=.35 (.54 for the three best, B=24.56, c=.72). N=20 (8 Experts mean Elo 2121; 7 Class A 1879; 5 Masters).
limits: Only 5 Masters, wide CIs on the Master game fit. From the table I get c x2.2 (Exp) and x13 (Masters); the text says 15.
agent_relevance: Constants are safe to quote. Masters' game-position fit is weak, so do not build a hard rule on c=.435.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models (COLM 2024), Appendix E and Table 3
finding: The 64% and 69.6% win rates are two measurements of the same 16-layer model under different Stockfish limits, so there is no contradiction. 64% is the headline result (time-limited Stockfish level 0). 69.6% is the baseline in the intervention table, where Stockfish was limited to 100,000 nodes per move to cut variance.
numbers: Headline: 8-layer 46%, 16-layer 64% vs Stockfish level 0 (about Elo 1300); legal moves 99.6% / 99.8%. Table 3 (5,000 games, 100,000 nodes): 16L standard 69.6 (none), 72.3 (positive skill vector), 11.9 (negative); 8L standard 49.6/54.8/5.5; 16L random board 16.7/43.2/5.9; 8L random board 15.7/31.3/3.6. Positive vector on random boards: x2.6 (16L), x2.0 (8L). Games stopped at 90 turns and scored by a 100-cp rule; win=1, draw=0.5.
limits: 'Random board' is a board reached after 20 random legal moves, not shuffled pieces, so it is an out-of-distribution start, not the De Groot scramble. The paper does not itself say this explains the 64 vs 69.6 gap; I infer it from Appendix E (engine limit differs).
agent_relevance: Closes the 64 vs 69.6 question. Scale (8L to 16L) raises standard win rate by 20 points but random-board win rate by 1 point: a machine echo of 'skill helps structured input far more than shuffled input'.

source: Song et al. (2025) Beyond Accuracy: A Geometric Stability Analysis of Large Language Models in Chess Evaluation
finding: Six frontier LLMs evaluated about 3,000 chess positions under invariant transformations. 180-degree rotation hurts most; left-right mirror and format change hurt much less. The authors read this as reliance on absolute square names.
numbers: Mean absolute error between evaluations of invariant pairs (cp), color swap / rotation / mirror / similarity / format / average: Claude Sonnet 4.5 199/627/196/318/62/280; Kimi K2 Turbo 368/726/95/329/36/311; DeepSeek Chat 254/997/235/400/121/402; Gemini 2.5 Flash 777/855/747/559/261/640; GPT-5.1 217/2531/181/298/48/655; Grok 4-1-Fast 786/1047/517/767/476/719. GPT-5.1 error on standard positions 362 cp.
limits: Measures evaluation consistency, not recall; no human baseline; one prompt format; hosted models change over time.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 6: LLM knowledge of board-like input is location and format specific (rotation worst), as location-specific chunks predict. Mirror is mostly tolerated, unlike the human quadrant-swap result, so the analogy is partial.

source: Liu et al. (2023, TACL 2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval: accuracy is best when the relevant item is at the start or end of the input and falls when it is in the middle, even for long-context models.
numbers: Abstract page only; no accuracies read. Tasks: multi-document QA and synthetic key-value retrieval.
limits: Abstract page read, not the full paper. 2023 models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: LLM retrieval is order and position sensitive, so place active chunks at the start or end of the prompt.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang & Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models (ICML 2024)
finding: Shuffling the order of premises, with no change in content, drops LLM accuracy a lot on deductive tasks and on reordered grade-school math. The gap grows with the number of rules.
numbers: Logical reasoning, 12 rules, forward vs shuffled: GPT-4-turbo 96.5->80.8%; PaLM 2-L 88.0->66.5%; Gemini 1.0 Pro 16.5->0.2%; GPT-3.5-turbo 30.0->1.2%. Gap vs rule count 4 to 12: GPT-4-turbo 0.2 -> 15.7 points; PaLM 2-L 0.2 -> 21.5. R-GSM (220 pairs): GPT-4-turbo 94.1->85.0%; PaLM 2-L 86.4->79.5%; Gemini 1.0 Pro 80.5->69.1%; GPT-3.5-turbo 67.3->51.8%.
limits: Numbers read through a page summary of the HTML version. 2024 models. Forward order matches proof order, so the effect is structure benefit, not pure position.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6 yes for order randomisation: it hurts multi-fact use, and order that follows the reasoning chain helps. The effect is small at 4 rules and large at 12, as a load account predicts.

source: Levy, Jacoby & Goldberg (2024) Same Task, More Tokens: the Impact of Input Length on the Reasoning Performance of LLMs (ACL 2024)
finding: With the task fixed and only irrelevant padding added, reasoning accuracy falls well before the context limit, and chain-of-thought does not remove the drop.
numbers: FLenQA: 3 tasks (MonoRel, People In Rooms, simplified Ruletaker), 100 base instances each; lengths about 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000 tokens; each point averages 300 samples. Mean accuracy over models 0.92 at 250 tokens, 0.68 at 3000. GPT-4 at 250 tokens: 1.00, 1.00, 0.98 (direct prompt). Key paragraphs last gave highest accuracy; some models did worse with them in the middle.
limits: Read from the HTML via a page summary; per-model 3000-token values only in figures. Padding is irrelevant text, not extra relevant chunks.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: more context hurts at a few thousand tokens. No test of a 3-4 chunk cap exists. This supports a small active set, not the exact number.

source: Hu et al. (2024) HiAgent: Hierarchical Working Memory Management for Solving Long-Horizon Agent Tasks (arXiv 2408.09559), ablations and decomposition control
finding: The full paper has one control that matters: subgoal planning without hiding old trajectories gains 30 points of success but is still 20 points below HiAgent. No other summarising scheme was compared.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo, AgentBoard, 5 tasks, max 30 steps. Overall: success +21%, progress +23.94%, steps -3.8, context -35%. Tyreworld ablation: HiAgent SR 60.0; without observation summarisation SR 30.0 (-30), steps 24.2, context +10.8%, time +22.5%; without trajectory retrieval SR 50.0 (-10); neither SR 30.0. Decomposition-only control: +30 SR vs STANDARD but 20 below HiAgent, runtime +5.7% and context +12.8% vs HiAgent. Blocksworld STANDARD executability below 10% after step 20; HiAgent above 80%. Gripper success 50 vs 50 (no gain).
limits: Tyreworld ablation success steps of 10 points suggest about 10 episodes. Single backbone. Gains vary by task. Not tested against other summarisers.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 only partly closed: there is a decomposition-only control but no equal-budget comparison with other summarisers inside this paper. See d09.

source: Sun et al. (2025) Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agent via Context-Folding (arXiv 2510.11967)
finding: An independent group tests the same idea (a finished sub-task branch is folded into a short summary) and compares it with a summarise-when-full agent at equal 32K context. Folding beats summarising even before RL.
numbers: Seed-OSS-36B; BrowseComp-Plus N=150 and SWE-Bench Verified N=500, pass@1. Prompt-only: ReAct 32K 0.286/0.436; ReAct 327K 0.478/0.552; Summary agent (32K x10 sessions) 0.386/0.488; Folding agent 0.420/0.492. After RL: Summary+GRPO 0.527/0.550; Folding+GRPO 0.567/0.564; Folding+FoldGRPO 0.620/0.580. Active context about 10x smaller than 327K ReAct. FoldGRPO adds +7.7 points on BrowseComp over plain GRPO.
limits: Table read from messy text extraction; I matched cells using the printed deltas to the 327K ReAct baseline. Best results use RL, which our scaffold will not. Prompt-only edge of folding over summarising is 3.4 points (BrowseComp) and 0.4 (SWE).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports sub-goal-close folding over generic summarise-when-full at equal context, but the prompt-only margin is small. Do not expect the RL gain.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents (arXiv 2506.15841)
finding: A constant-size internal state replaces the growing history. In a 16-objective multi-hop QA task a 7B model with this state beats a 14B model with full history, plain truncation and an external-memory baseline.
numbers: Table 1 (EM / peak tokens in hundreds): 16-objective MEM1-QA 1.97 / 10.4; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct 0.567 / 38.4; Qwen2.5-7B 0.165 / 43.3; 7B with A-MEM 0.730 / 18.8; 7B with truncation 0.396 / 13.3; Search-R1 0.009; DeepResearcher 0.071. 2-objective: 14B 0.732 vs MEM1-QA 0.709. MEM1 uses 27.1% of the peak tokens and 29.3% of the inference time of the 14B at 16 objectives. Others' peak tokens grow near linearly with objectives; MEM1 almost flat.
limits: MEM1 is RL-trained, so the gain is not a pure scaffold effect. EM above 1 is a count of correct answers over objectives, not a percent.
agent_relevance: Supports a compact consolidated state over a raw log (gaps 3 and 4), but the gain needs the model to learn what to keep.

source: Lane & Chang (2018) Chess knowledge predicts chess memory even after controlling for chess experience: evidence for the role of high-level processes (Memory & Cognition)
finding: An independent group tests template theory against a conceptual-knowledge account. Declarative chess knowledge predicts position memory beyond experience, and fluid intelligence adds more. The authors say their literature review favours the high-level account over template theory.
numbers: N=79 chess players. Chess knowledge correlated .67 with chess memory and explained 16% of variance after controlling for chess experience; fluid intelligence added 13%.
quote: both high-level conceptual processing and low-level recognition of familiar patterns play important roles in memory for chess positions
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC; full text not opened. Correlational. A knowledge test is not independent of pattern knowledge.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: an outside group partly disagrees with pure template theory. Our memory should hold concept-level notes as well as patterns.

source: Saariluoma & Laine (2001) as reported by Gobet (2001) Chunk hierarchies and retrieval structures: comments on Saariluoma and Laine (Scand J Psychol 42, 149-155)
finding: An independent lab trained two people on chess recall. Both improved fast then slowly (power or log curves) and both gained a little on random positions, as chunking predicts. Saariluoma and Laine argued frequency-based learning fits better than proximity-based learning; Gobet shows CHREST (proximity-based) fits as well.
numbers: N=2 trained subjects. CHREST simulation: 500 training positions from 67 games gave 708 templates and recall under 45%; about 10,000 chunks gave about 60%; about 300,000 chunks are needed for master level.
limits: N=2; both subjects knew some chess; no error or strategy data; the model comparison is argued by the CHREST author. Read via Gobet's comment, not the original paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: independent support for the shape of the learning curve, but the rival 'frequency' mechanism is not excluded. Weak replication.

source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving (Thinking & Reasoning 3, 291-313), SEARCH model
finding: Re-reading SEARCH: mean depth rises as a power function of net size and flattens, and human data show only a weak skill-depth relation. A bigger pattern store gives diminishing depth gains.
numbers: 1,000 episodes per net size. Mean depth: under 1 ply with no chunks; about 2.5 plies at 1,000 chunks; about 4 at about 30,000 (expert); over 5 above 100,000 (grandmaster). Human: Holding's calculation on de Groot gave 4.8 (experts) and 5.3 plies (grandmasters); Charness-based regression about 2.3 plies at Elo 1300, 4.1 at 2000, 5.7 at grandmaster. Saariluoma (1990): IMs and GMs searched less than Masters.
limits: Simulation with assumed parameters; no single human study spans novice to GM; random variation at large nets.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 (model answer only): most depth gain arrives in the first few thousand patterns, then slowly. No LLM measurement exists. A prediction, not a test.

source: Chassy, Lahaye & Gobet (2023) Templates but not emotions facilitate the information flow between long-term and working memory: a Sternberg study with chess experts (Journal of Expertise 6(1))
finding: Memory scanning is faster for experts even with more to hold, which fits templates changing how long-term memory is accessed. Emotion priming had no reliable effect.
numbers: N=60 (30 club, 30 expert), memory load 3, 4 or 5 items. Mean hit ratio .89 (SD .15). Mean RT on correct trials 3.32 s (SD 1.21). Experts 3.02 s vs club 3.62 s (600 ms faster). Probe present 3.20 s vs absent 3.44 s. Load effect F(1,54)=12.70, p<.001.
limits: Gobet is a co-author, so not independent. RT inference is indirect. Emotion manipulation was weak.
agent_relevance: Weak. Suggests retrieval from a well-formed store is faster, not slower. No direct use.

source: Gobet (2001) comment on Saariluoma & Laine: curve fits cannot separate learning mechanisms
finding: Power and log functions describe both the rival model and CHREST well for game positions, but not for random positions. Curve fit alone cannot decide between learning mechanisms, and the author asks for data on chunk structure and error types.
limits: Commentary by the author of one of the models.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations stay open. Do not claim chunk theory has beaten frequency-based learning.

source: CHESS-WORLD-MODEL (2026): a 10M-game benchmark for exact state tracking from chess move sequences (arXiv 2605.30100)
finding: Models trained on 10M real games are tested on held-out real games and on uniformly random legal play. The random split stays discriminative up to 40M parameters while real-game performance saturates above 18M. Shuffled-style data exposes failures that scale hides on in-distribution data.
numbers: Recurrent models beat the Transformer at 3M and 8M parameters. Real-game performance saturates above 18M; random-uniform split discriminative to 40M. All 1,968 move tokens in the random test also occur in training (9.61% of the 20,480-token vocabulary), which rules out an unseen-token explanation. Per-model exact-state table was not parsed.
limits: Chess only; state tracking, not memory recall; exact accuracy tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a machine version of the random-position effect. No structured-versus-shuffled long-context recall test was found in this search.

source: Gong, Wan & Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (arXiv 2305.03731)
finding: ChatGPT shows an n-back capacity limit like humans in verbal and spatial versions, with variants (noise, feedback, chain-of-thought). Human accuracy typically drops at 3-back. GPT-4 was not tested above n=3 because of cost, so its limit is unknown.
numbers: Per-condition hit, false alarm and d' values are only in figures that did not extract as text; exact values not read this session.
limits: n-back tests updating and attention, not chunk capacity; no chunking manipulation, so it cannot tell a 4-chunk cap from a token cap.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no study sets a working-set cap in chunk units for an LLM scaffold. Keep 3-4 as a design hypothesis to test.

source: Gobet, Lane & Lloyd-Kelly (2015) Chunks, schemata, and retrieval structures: past and current computational models (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Review of computational chunk models. It argues verbal theories are weak (long-term working memory applied to Saariluoma's dictation task without a model) and notes that 'chunk' means a declarative unit in ACT-R and a procedural unit in Soar.
numbers: No new experimental numbers in the parts read.
limits: Written by the CHREST group. Part of the text read; no abstract block in the XML.
agent_relevance: Terminology warning for our schema: define 'chunk' as a note with slots, not any unit.
